summary: Codex is built around a coherent, defense-in-depth security design: everything the model emits (shell commands, patches, MCP tool calls) must pass an approval stage and then runs inside an OS-level sandbox whose default policy is read-only with no network. The layers compose explicitly - a per-project trust boundary picks the approval default, a Starlark exec-policy classifies commands as allow/prompt/forbidden, an optional model-based 'guardian' reviewer fails closed, and the OS layer (deny-default seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap+seccomp+no_new_privs on Linux, restricted token on Windows) catches whatever the approval layer waves through. Escape hatches are deliberate, loudly named (--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox / --yolo), and enterprise requirements layers (MDM, requirements.toml, backend-delivered) can pin approval policy, permission profiles, MCP servers, plugin marketplaces and network constraints. The visible soft spots are defaults rather than missing walls: model-run commands inherit the user's full environment (the built-in *KEY*/*SECRET*/*TOKEN* filter ships disabled), the Windows sandbox defaults to disabled (compensated by approval prompts), MCP tools in the default Auto mode are auto-approved on the basis of server-self-declared annotations, and plugin marketplace source restrictions are opt-in.

findings.title: Trust boundary map: model output, MCP servers, plugins, hooks, project files, and the network all cross explicit gates
findings.description: The design treats six inputs as untrusted: (1) model output - every tool call is driven through a single orchestrator that sequences approval, sandbox selection, and sandboxed execution; (2) MCP servers - tool calls pass a per-server approval mode; (3) plugins/marketplaces - installation is policy-checked and plugin-supplied hooks and commands run under the same exec gates; (4) hooks - config-file hooks require a persisted trust hash before they execute; (5) the project itself - per-project trust levels change the approval default; (6) network traffic - an in-process proxy applies deny-capable domain and method policy, and the OS sandbox blocks network entirely by default. The two central chokepoints are core/src/tools/orchestrator.rs (all tool runtimes) and core/src/tools/approvals.rs (all approval routing, including guardian and MCP flows), which keeps the boundary checks in one place instead of scattered per tool.

findings.title: Per-project trust levels drive approval defaults, and privilege-escalation paths inside the workspace stay read-only
findings.description: The workspace itself is a trust boundary in two directions. Inbound: a project marked untrusted defaults to the internal AskForApproval::UnlessTrusted policy (every command needs approval unless an exec-policy rule allows it), while a trusted project defaults to OnRequest. Outbound: even when a root is writable, WritableRoot carves out read-only subpaths and protected metadata names specifically so the agent cannot edit files that would escalate its own privileges on a later run - the doc comment names .codex, .git and .git/hooks. This shows the authors modeled the 'agent writes a git hook that runs unsandboxed later' loop, a second-order threat many agent designs miss.

evidence.note: untrusted projects default to approval-for-everything

findings.title: OS sandbox: deny-default seatbelt (macOS), bubblewrap + seccomp + no_new_privs (Linux), restricted token (Windows); read-only is the policy default
findings.description: Command execution confinement is per-OS and closed-by-default. macOS generates an SBPL profile starting from '(deny default)' (modeled on Chrome's sandbox policy) and runs it via a pinned /usr/bin/sandbox-exec - the constant's comment explains PATH-injection is out of scope because tampering with /usr/bin implies root. Linux uses a dedicated codex-linux-sandbox helper: bubblewrap for filesystem isolation plus in-process no_new_privs and a network seccomp filter when network is disabled; the bundled bubblewrap binary is sha256-verified before use. Windows uses a restricted-token sandbox when enabled. The configured SandboxMode defaults to ReadOnly, and both ReadOnly and WorkspaceWrite default to network_access=false, so an unconfigured install runs model commands with no writes outside temp and no network.

evidence.note: macOS profile is closed-by-default

findings.title: Windows sandbox defaults to Disabled; the compensating control is approval prompts, not confinement
findings.description: WindowsSandboxLevel defaults to Disabled, and get_platform_sandbox returns None on Windows unless the sandbox is explicitly enabled - unlike macOS and Linux where a platform sandbox is always available. The design compensates rather than silently degrading: assess_patch_safety only auto-approves in-workspace writes when a platform sandbox exists, otherwise it falls back to asking the user (or rejecting under Never/Granular policies). So Windows users get a noisier, human-gated experience instead of a weaker silent one - a defensible trade-off, but it means the single wall on default Windows installs is user judgment on approval prompts, and users who approve routinely get no second layer.

evidence.note: off unless configured

findings.recommendation: Consider enabling the restricted-token sandbox by default on supported Windows versions once mature, or surface the reduced-confinement state prominently in the UI so Windows users understand approvals are the only wall.

findings.title: Escape hatches are explicit, loudly named, and consent-gated; escalation preserves denied-read restrictions
findings.description: Four deliberate bypasses exist. (1) --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox (alias --yolo) maps directly to AskForApproval::Never plus SandboxMode::DangerFullAccess; its help text says it is 'EXTREMELY DANGEROUS' and intended for externally sandboxed environments. (2) --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust skips the hook trust-hash requirement. (3) The external-sandbox policy declares 'already sandboxed elsewhere' and drops the Codex filesystem sandbox. (4) Per-command escalation: a model request for escalated permissions can bypass the sandbox for the first attempt, but only after passing the approval stage, and unsandboxed_execution_allowed refuses the bypass whenever the policy carries denied-read paths, because only the sandbox enforces those - an unusually careful composition rule. All hatches require an explicit flag or config choice by the operator; none is reachable by model output alone.

findings.title: Pre-main process hardening: ptrace-attach denied, core dumps disabled, LD_/DYLD_ scrubbed
findings.description: A dedicated process-hardening crate runs before main() (via #[ctor]) and hardens the Codex process itself, not just its children: it marks the process non-dumpable / denies ptrace attach on Linux and macOS, sets the core-file size limit to zero (so tokens in memory don't land in core dumps), and removes loader-injection variables (LD_*, DYLD_*) - noting that official MUSL-linked releases ignore LD_PRELOAD anyway. Failures exit the process with dedicated exit codes rather than continuing unhardened. This protects credentials and session state in the agent's own address space from same-user attackers and accidental disclosure.

evidence.note: self-hardening entry point, called pre-main

findings.title: Approval model: four policy modes, an allow/prompt/forbidden exec-policy, and a fail-closed model-based guardian reviewer
findings.description: The permission model composes three mechanisms. AskForApproval has four modes - UnlessTrusted (everything prompts), OnRequest (default; prompts whenever the filesystem sandbox is restricted), Granular (per-category booleans whose 'false' means auto-reject, not silently allow), and Never (failures return to the model, and anything that would have prompted is rejected). Exec-policy rules, written in Starlark and stored under CODEX_HOME/rules, classify commands as Allow / Prompt / Forbidden; Prompt under approval_policy=never is rejected outright, so the two systems compose fail-closed. Finally, an optional guardian reviewer ('--approve-for-me') routes on-request approvals to a dedicated model session that reconstructs the transcript, assesses the exact planned action, and explicitly fails closed on timeout, execution failure, or malformed output. Approvals are cached by canonicalized command so retries do not re-prompt.

findings.title: Auth design: PKCE OAuth on a localhost callback, pluggable credential stores, and hygiene-checked workload-identity exchange
findings.description: Identity has three flows. Interactive ChatGPT sign-in uses OAuth authorization-code with PKCE S256 and a short-lived localhost callback server (default port 1455, redirect http://localhost:.../auth/callback), so no client secret exists on the machine. API-key auth talks to api.openai.com directly. For fleet deployments, the workload-identity crate exchanges a JWT bearer for short-lived access tokens, caching them only in memory; validate_token_url rejects token URLs carrying credentials, query or fragment and requires https except for loopback http - the risk-synthesis scan flagged this security-critical file as single-owner (bus factor). Enterprise requirements can force allowed_login_methods and pin allowed ChatGPT workspaces.

findings.title: Enterprise requirements layers (MDM, requirements.toml, backend-delivered) can pin nearly every security-relevant knob
findings.description: A dedicated requirements system lets administrators constrain the security posture from outside the user's config: requirement sources include macOS MDM managed preferences, a system requirements.toml, backend-delivered enterprise-managed layers, and legacy managed_config.toml. ConfigRequirements can constrain (not just default) the approval policy, approvals reviewer, permission profile and Windows sandbox mode; pin allowed login methods and ChatGPT workspaces; require specific MCP servers, plugins and marketplace sources; inject an exec policy; and impose network and filesystem constraints. Config resolution enforces these via Constrained::can_set - a user default that violates a requirement is overridden with a warning. This is the mechanism that turns the local trust model into something an organization can rely on.

evidence.note: the full admin-constrainable surface (lines 156-190)
approval policy is a constraint, not just a default
backend-delivered managed layer as a requirement source

findings.title: Model-run commands inherit the user's full environment by default; the built-in secret-name filter ships disabled
findings.description: The shell environment policy that builds the environment for model-executed commands defaults to inherit=All with ignore_default_excludes=true. The code contains a ready-made default exclude list - case-insensitive *KEY*, *SECRET*, *TOKEN* patterns - but it only applies when a user explicitly sets ignore_default_excludes=false, so a stock install passes OPENAI_API_KEY, AWS credentials, and any other secrets in the parent environment into every approved or sandboxed command the model runs. The OS sandbox does not help here: the environment is handed to the child regardless of filesystem policy. Only Codex's own sensitive launch context (exec-server noise token, workload-identity token file path, etc.) is force-scrubbed via NON_INHERITABLE_ENV_VARS. The escape is one prompt-injected `env` or `printenv` away from putting the user's secrets into model context and, with network enabled, exfiltration. This is a deliberate compatibility choice (builds break when *KEY* vars vanish), but it is the weakest default in an otherwise closed-by-default design.

evidence.note: full inheritance and the secret filter off, both by default
the dormant built-in secret filter
only Codex-internal tokens are always scrubbed

findings.recommendation: Flip ignore_default_excludes to false by default (or at minimum for untrusted projects), with a first-run notice and an easy opt-out; alternatively redact matching values from model-visible command output the way user prompts are redacted in telemetry.

findings.title: Secrets at rest: auth.json written 0600 with optional keyring/ephemeral backends; best-effort regex redaction for text surfaces
findings.description: Credential storage is a pluggable design: AuthCredentialsStoreMode defaults to File (CODEX_HOME/auth.json, written with mode 0o600 on Unix), with Keyring (platform secret service via the keyring-store crate; fail if unavailable), Auto (keyring with file fallback) and Ephemeral (memory-only) modes - and enterprise requirements can force the store mode. A separate secrets crate provides a local secrets backend keyed through the OS keyring and a redact_secrets sanitizer that strips OpenAI keys (sk-...), AWS access key IDs, bearer tokens, and generic api_key/token/secret/password assignments from strings on a best-effort basis. Telemetry-side prompt redaction ([REDACTED] unless otel.log_user_prompt=true) was documented by the observability scan; this scanner confirms the storage side matches: nothing stores tokens world-readable, and memory-only operation is a supported first-class mode.

findings.title: Model-proposed commands and patches are parsed, canonicalized, and path-normalized before any yes/no decision
findings.description: The two highest-volume untrusted inputs - shell command vectors and apply_patch actions - are validated structurally before policy is applied. Commands are parsed into plain command lists (including unwrapping shell -lc forms) so exec-policy rules match real executables rather than raw strings, and are canonicalized before approval caching so a cached 'yes' cannot be replayed against a materially different command. Patches are checked by is_write_patch_constrained_to_writable_paths, which normalizes each affected path component-wise (rejecting traversal above the writable root via ParentDir handling) before comparing against writable roots; the code comments explicitly note that even a passing check still runs apply_patch inside the sandbox because paths may be hard links to files outside the roots - validation is treated as advisory, with the sandbox as the enforcement layer. That 'validate but still sandbox' stance is the right one for canonicalization-resistant filesystems.

findings.title: MCP tool auto-approval trusts server-self-declared annotations in the default Auto mode
findings.description: MCP tool calls pass an approval gate whose default mode is AppToolApproval::Auto. Auto decides using the tool's own annotations, which the MCP server itself supplies: destructive_hint=true always prompts, absent hints conservatively prompt (destructive and open-world both default to true), but read_only_hint=true short-circuits to no approval. That means a configured-but-malicious or compromised MCP server can label any tool read-only and have the model invoke it without a human gate - the annotation is a claim by the very party the gate is supposed to check. The blast radius is bounded: the server executes the tool on its own side regardless of approval, per-server approval_mode can be set to Prompt/Writes, restrict_to combines policies conservatively (Auto vs Writes intersects to Prompt), and enterprise requirements can pin the allowed MCP server set. Still, the default places the trust decision at configuration time while the per-call gate quietly defers to the counterparty's self-description.

evidence.note: Auto is the default approval mode
server-claimed read_only_hint suppresses the approval prompt

findings.recommendation: Document that Auto trusts server annotations, and consider treating first-party-unverified servers' read_only_hint as Prompt (or requiring one-time per-tool consent) so the self-declaration only relaxes prompting for servers the user has explicitly trusted.

findings.title: Plugin marketplace source restriction is opt-in: unmanaged installs accept any marketplace or git source
findings.description: The plugin subsystem has a real allowlist mechanism - MarketplacePolicy compiled from enterprise requirements can restrict installs to named allowed sources (by kind, URL, ref, host pattern) and blocks installs from unconfigured marketplaces while restrictions are active - but it activates only when requirements set restrict_to_allowed_sources=true; the code defaults it to false, leaving unmanaged installs free to add arbitrary marketplaces and git sources. There is no signature or checksum verification of plugin content at install time (the Sha256 use in the plugin store is cache-keying, not integrity checking); trust rests on the source URL the user chose plus the fact that plugin-supplied commands and hooks still run behind the exec-approval and sandbox gates, and plugin hooks still need the hook trust hash. For a system whose plugins can contribute hooks, commands, and MCP servers, install-time trust is the thinnest of the third-party layers.

evidence.note: restriction is off unless an admin requirement enables it
the managed allowlist that would hold the missing policy for unmanaged users

findings.recommendation: Add content integrity for plugin installs (pin a commit/digest at install time and verify on upgrade), and consider a first-use consent screen for non-curated marketplaces summarizing what the plugin will contribute (hooks, MCP servers, commands).

findings.title: Runtime code trust: hooks gated on a persisted config hash; bundled bubblewrap sha256-verified; sandbox-exec pinned to /usr/bin
findings.description: Three load-time trust mechanisms guard code Codex did not ship in its own binary. Config-defined hooks (which execute arbitrary commands on agent events) run only when their current config hash matches a previously persisted trusted_hash - editing a hook invalidates its trust until re-approved - with managed (admin-delivered) hooks implicitly trusted and a --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust flag as the explicit escape. The bundled bubblewrap binary that implements Linux filesystem isolation is verified against a build-time sha256 before execution, with a dedicated exit code on mismatch, so a swapped helper cannot silently weaken the sandbox. On macOS the sandbox is executed only via the absolute path /usr/bin/sandbox-exec, never a PATH lookup. Together these close the 'the sandbox itself is the supply chain' loop; installer/update trust on the distribution side (signing, notarization, mutable install.sh) was covered by the cicd-scan.

evidence.note: hook trust is a hash pin over the hook's configuration

findings.title: Network egress: OS-level deny by default, with an in-process policy proxy as the managed alternative
findings.description: Network is treated as a boundary with two enforcement styles. By default the OS sandbox blocks it outright: both ReadOnly and WorkspaceWrite policies default network_access to false, Linux installs a network seccomp filter when disabled, and the macOS profile only appends network allowances (scoped to system services and proxy sockets) when access is enabled. When network is granted under management, traffic is steered through the codex network-proxy, which applies domain allow/deny entries, unix-socket permissions, and a NetworkMode where Limited restricts HTTP to GET/HEAD/OPTIONS and blocks HTTPS CONNECT unless MITM is enabled so method policy can be enforced on inner requests; policy decisions are explicit Allow/Deny values with attributed reasons. Notably NetworkMode itself defaults to Full - the proxy's job in the default case is attribution and domain policy, not method restriction - so the effective network posture depends on which layer (sandbox off-switch vs proxy policy) a deployment leans on.

Limited mode is read-only HTTP; Full (the default, line 306-307) tunnels everything

findings.title: Posture: genuine defense in depth against the model itself; residual risk concentrates in defaults and configured-third-party trust
findings.description: The trust model in three sentences: the model is the primary adversary, and everything it emits crosses an approval gate (policy modes, Starlark exec rules, optional fail-closed guardian model) before running inside a closed-by-default OS sandbox that also protects the agent's own escalation paths (.git/hooks, .codex); the user is the root of trust, with explicit, loudly-named flags as the only way to remove layers; organizations can override the user through layered managed requirements. Depth is real - approval, sandbox, exec-policy and hardening are independent walls, and the code repeatedly refuses to let one layer's bypass drop another's guarantees (denied reads survive escalation, patches run sandboxed even when path checks pass). What the design visibly does not defend by default: secrets in the inherited environment (the one boundary crossed unchecked - see the medium finding), Windows confinement (sandbox off, human wall only), and parties the user configured once and forgot - MCP servers whose self-declared annotations relax prompting, and plugin marketplaces installable from any source. A reviewer should probe next: the annotation-trust path end-to-end with a hostile MCP server, prompt-injection-driven env exfiltration under workspace-write with network enabled, and the guardian's containment (its review session inherits the parent's managed network). Strength-side found-while-reading: no committed credentials or no-op checks were encountered; the only embedded key is the client-side Statsig key already reported by the observability scan.
